subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Transmission Spectroscopy
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Transmission Spectroscopy.

hook.text: When an exoplanet transits its star, starlight filters through its atmosphere. Each gas leaves a unique fingerprint.

buildup.text: Different molecules absorb specific wavelengths. By comparing starlight during and outside transit, we read the atmosphere.

discovery.text: Sodium was the first molecule detected in an exoplanet atmosphere in 2001—on the hot Jupiter HD 209458b.

twist.text: Clouds and hazes can block the signal, producing flat, featureless spectra. Many early targets were frustratingly opaque.

climax.text: JWST's infrared power cuts through clouds much better. It's already detecting water, CO₂, and more on distant worlds.

punchline.text: Starlight through alien air. Each wavelength tells us what that world breathes.

quiz.question: How does transmission spectroscopy reveal an exoplanet's atmosphere?
options: Starlight filtered through the planet's atmosphere shows absorption lines from its gases
Telescopes photograph the atmosphere directly and analyze its color
Radio signals bounced off the planet's surface reveal atmospheric density

details.summary: Transmission spectroscopy analyzes starlight filtered through a transiting exoplanet's atmosphere. Different elements and molecules absorb specific wavelengths, leaving fingerprints in the light spectrum.
details.whyItMatters: Transmission spectroscopy is the primary tool for characterizing exoplanet atmospheres. It bridges the gap between detecting planets and understanding what they're made of — a key step toward identifying habitable worlds.
takeaways: Analyzes starlight passing through a planet's atmosphere during transit
JWST is dramatically expanding atmospheric characterization

faq.question: What has JWST detected in exoplanet atmospheres?
faq.answer: JWST detected carbon dioxide in WASP-39b's atmosphere — the first unambiguous CO₂ detection. It has also identified water vapor, sulfur dioxide (indicating photochemistry), and silicate clouds.

faq.question: Could transmission spectroscopy detect signs of life?
faq.answer: Potentially. Biosignature gases like oxygen combined with methane (a thermodynamic disequilibrium) could indicate biology. However, false positives exist — abiotic processes can produce similar signals.
